add_option: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)
x: Hyderabad State (the Asaf Jahi dominion) was founded by Chin Qilich Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, in 1724, and none of the printed names is he. Quli Qutb Shah founded only Hyderabad city (1591), and Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were later claimants.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17 (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded Hyderabad in 1724); PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58

x: The tithe was the tax (about one-tenth of produce) that the Church collected in pre-revolutionary France. The taille was a direct tax paid to the state, the livre was the currency, and jizya was a Muslim poll tax.
source: NCERT Class IX History ch.1 'The French Revolution' (tithes, taille)

x: The order of reigns is Bahadur Shah I (1707-12), Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Farrukhsiyar (1713-19), Muhammad Shah (1719-48) and Shah Alam II (1759-1806). The other options swap Farrukhsiyar and Muhammad Shah or put Bahadur Shah last.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20-21

x: Jahandar Shah was defeated in 1713 by his nephew Farrukhsiyar, who was backed by the Sayyid brothers, and was then killed. He was not deposed by his own wazir, Zulfiqar Khan.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.39; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20

x: Shah Alam II did spend his first years away from Delhi, out of fear of his wazir Imad-ul-Mulk and the court intrigue, living at Allahabad after Buxar. North-western invasions were a real danger, but they were not why he stayed away, so both are true and R does not explain A (UPSC key b).
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.41; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 0

x: Nadir Shah invaded in 1739 and defeated Muhammad Shah (1719-48) at Karnal. Ahmad Shah, Alamgir II and Rafi-ud-Darajat ruled at other times.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21

x: The order is Bahadur Shah I (1707-12), then Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Farrukhsiyar (1713-19) and Muhammad Shah (1719-48), which gives III, II, I, IV.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20-21

x: By Bahadur Shah Zafar's time the emperor's real authority ran only from his Red Fort in Delhi to Palam, which is the 'Chandni Chowk (Lal Qila) to Palam' option. The printed key 'Delhi to Bihar' has no basis, and the printed explanation was about Awadh.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahadur_Shah_Zafar (empire reduced to Delhi and the territory as far as Palam); ranasafvi.com (saying 'az Dilli ta Palam')
evidence: vajiramandravi.com Bahadur Shah Zafar (authority contracted to Delhi and Palam)
dispute: Most guides: 'Chandni Chowk / Delhi to Palam'. Strictly, the saying 'Sultanat-e-Shah Alam, az Dilli ta Palam' was first made of Shah Alam II, and it was later applied to Zafar.

x: Under Ahmad Shah (1748-54) the government was left to the queen mother Udham Bai and her favourite, the eunuch Javed Khan, which is the 'eunuchs and ladies' rule. Muhammad Shah was the pleasure-loving 'Rangeela', but the eunuch-and-harem government belongs to Ahmad Shah's reign.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.117; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.40; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) ch.4 (Udham Bai and the eunuch Javid Khan)
evidence: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) ch.4
dispute: Some guides (and the old app key) give Muhammad Shah. PMF and Spectrum tie the rule of Udham Bai and the eunuch Javed Khan to Ahmad Shah.

x: Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Muhammad Shah (1719-48), Ahmad Shah (1748-54) and Alamgir II (1754-59) gives B, A, D, C.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20-21

x: Wazir Ghaziuddin (Imad-ul-Mulk), who had murdered Alamgir II, kept Ali Gauhar (Shah Alam II) out of Delhi. He entered his capital only in 1772 with Maratha help (Mahadji Scindia).
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.41; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 0

x: Muhammad Shah was the last Mughal emperor to sit on the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus), which Nadir Shah carried away in 1739.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 0

x: Aurangzeb was succeeded in 1707 by his son Muazzam as Bahadur Shah I (1707-12). Jahandar Shah, Muhammad Shah and Akbar II came later.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20

x: Bahadur Shah I released Shahu, Sambhaji's son, in 1707. Jizya was abolished only after his reign (1713), and he did not revive Holi at court or support sati.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20 (he released Shahuji)

x: Roshan Akhtar was the personal name of Muhammad Shah, later nicknamed 'Rangeela'.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.40; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 0

x: Muhammad Shah ruled for about 29 years (1719-48), the longest among these. Bahadur Shah I ruled about 5 years, Jahandar Shah 1 and Farrukhsiyar 6.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20-21

x: Nadir Shah attacked in 1739, when Muhammad Shah was emperor, and defeated him at Karnal before sacking Delhi.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21

x: Ahmad Shah (1748-54) left the government to the queen mother Udham Bai and the eunuch Javed Khan, so eunuchs and ladies dominated his court. Muhammad Shah, the tempting option, was the pleasure-loving 'Rangeela', but this coterie rule belongs to Ahmad Shah's reign.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.117; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.40; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) ch.4
evidence: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) ch.4

x: Plassey (1757) was fought in the reign of Alamgir II (1754-59). Ahmad Shah's reign ended in 1754 and Shah Alam II's began in 1759.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21 and p.18 (Plassey 1757)

x: The Rohilla Ghulam Qadir blinded Shah Alam II, in 1788 (the stem's 1780 is a misprint). Najib-ud-Daulah was his grandfather, and Mahadji Scindia later punished Ghulam Qadir.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 0; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.41

x: Bahadur Shah (Zafar, Bahadur Shah II) was the last Mughal emperor, exiled to Rangoon after 1857. He was not a Lodi, and not a successor of Sher Shah or Shivaji.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21

x: Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Muhammad Shah (1719-48), Ahmad Shah (1748-54) and Alamgir II (1754-59) gives II, I, IV, III.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.20-21

x: Bahadur Shah Zafar (II) succeeded his father Akbar Shah II (1806-37) in 1837.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.21

x: Muhammad Shah (1719-48) was called 'Rangeela' for his luxurious, pleasure-loving life. Farrukhsiyar and the two Rafis were the Sayyids' short-lived puppets.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.40; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) ch.4

x: Muhammad Shah (1719-48) was nicknamed 'Rangeela' for his luxurious life and neglect of administration.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.40

x: The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) was fought between Ahmad Shah Abdali and the Marathas. Akbar vs Hemu was Panipat II (1556).
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.18 (1761 Third Battle of Panipat: Marathas defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali)

x: Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried away the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne. Abdali and Timur are the tempting wrong options.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.42; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 3

x: Abdali left the Rohilla chief Najib Khan (Najib-ud-Daulah) at Delhi in 1757 as his trusted agent and Mir Bakhshi, and Najib invited him back before Panipat. Ghulam Qadir was Najib's grandson, and Ali Muhammad Khan founded Rohilkhand.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.43

x: Nadir Shah defeated Muhammad Shah at Karnal in 1739 and then sacked Delhi. Panipat is the tempting option, but it was the site of Abdali's 1761 battle.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.42; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 3

x: Only (a) is right: Hyderabad was founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk. Bengal's founder was Murshid Quli Khan (not Saadat Ali Khan), and Awadh's was Saadat Khan (not Murshid Quli Khan).
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58-64

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda in 1724 and became virtually independent, so 1724 is Hyderabad State's founding year.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17 (founded the state of Hyderabad in 1724)

x: Husain Ali Khan was a Sayyid brother, Murshid Quli Khan ruled Bengal, Chin Qilich Khan was the Nizam of Hyderabad and Safdar Jung the Nawab of Awadh, which gives A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.
source: Rocket Sheets Indian History 02 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.9; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17, p.36

x: Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the state of Hyderabad in 1724. Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were his successors and rivals after 1748, and Zulfiqar Khan only envisaged the Deccan state.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17, p.35; Rocket Sheets Indian History 02 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.9

x: Murshid Quli Khan, Diwan (1700) and then Nazim of Bengal, introduced revenue farming (ijaradari). Alivardi Khan, Sarfaraz Khan and Siraj-ud-Daulah came later.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.64; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 5

x: Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the independent Hyderabad state in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda. Qamaruddin Khan, Muhammad Amin Khan and Asad Khan were other nobles.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58

x: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk, governor from 1722, founded the independent state of Awadh, and he sided with Muhammad Shah in the plot against the Sayyid brothers, so both statements are correct.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.36; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.61

x: Safdar Jung, Saadat Khan's nephew and son-in-law and Nawab of Awadh, was made the Mughal Wazir (1748), which is why the Awadh Nawabs were styled Nawab Wazir. Saadat Khan never held the wazirship.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17, p.36 (Safdarjung was made the wazir)
dispute: Most keys: Safdar Jung. His son Shuja-ud-Daula was also later made Wazir (NextGen p.17, p.36).

x: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk, Subedar of Awadh from 1722, was the first Nawab of Awadh, which is the official CDS 2018 answer. Safdar Jung (the second Nawab) was the first to be the Mughal Wazir.
source: CDS-II 2018 answer key (examrobot.com, testbook.com); PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.61
dispute: Official key: Saadat Khan (first Nawab). Strictly, the 'Wazir' title began with his successor Safdar Jung (Mughal Wazir from 1748).

x: Saadat Khan founded the independent state of Awadh in Muhammad Shah's reign. Nizam-ul-Mulk founded Hyderabad, Alivardi Khan was a Nawab of Bengal, and Yusuf Adil Shah founded Bijapur.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.36

x: Sawai Jai Singh II built observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura, so all four listed places are correct.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.37

x: Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber built the Jantar Mantar at Delhi (1724), one of his five observatories. Suraj Mal was the Jat ruler of Bharatpur.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.37; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.83

x: Sawai Jai Singh of Jaipur drew up the astronomical tables Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi, named after Emperor Muhammad Shah.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.37 (drew up a set of tables); PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.83

x: The Marathas were the strongest native power after the Mughal decline, but they had no concept of a united Indian nation. Their sardars lacked the unity and programme needed for an all-India empire, so A is true and R is false.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.66; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 3

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, who founded Hyderabad State in 1724, died in 1748.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58 (1724-48)

x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi (Nizam-ul-Mulk, Asaf Jah I) founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724. Nizam Ali Khan, Salabat Jung and Nasir Jung were his sons.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6

x: Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911-48) was the seventh and last Nizam of Hyderabad; Operation Polo ended his rule in 1948. Mir Qamar-ud-din was the first Nizam, and Nizam Ali Khan the second.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osman_Ali_Khan

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded the Asaf Jahi (Asafzahi) dynasty of Hyderabad. The Qutb Shahis were the earlier Golconda dynasty.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17; Rocket Sheets Indian History 02 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.9

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724. Salar Jung was a 19th-century minister and Nizam Ali the second Nizam.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17

x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58

x: Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II, 1762-1803) accepted Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, the first ruler to do so. Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam and Nizam-ul-Mulk the first.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.39 (Wellesley's subsidiary alliance)

x: Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911-48), founder of Osmania University, was the seventh and last Asaf Jahi Nizam. Afzal-ud-Daula and Mahbub Ali Khan came earlier.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6

x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Siddiqi (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty and was the first Nizam. Hyderabad city, however, was founded in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, not in Nizam-ul-Mulk's time, so only statement I is correct.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724; 1748 is the year he died.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.17

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk ruled from 1724 until his death in 1748.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58 (1724-48)

x: Kilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) was not Mubariz Khan; Mubariz was the Mughal governor he defeated at Shakar Kheda (1724), so (ii) is true. The title Asaf Jah came from Muhammad Shah (1725), not Zulfiqar Khan, so (i) and (iii) are untrue.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 6; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.58

x: Irfan Habib (The Agrarian System of Mughal India) argued that the Mughal state was itself the principal instrument of exploitation, the root of the agrarian crisis. Satish Chandra stressed the jagirdari crisis and Athar Ali the nobility.
source: PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.48; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.14

x: Genghis Khan reached the Indus under Iltutmish (1221), Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, Nadir Shah came in 1739 and Abdali from 1748, so the order is 2, 4, 3, 1.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 139 sub 3; PMF Modern History 01 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-01.txt) p.42-43

x: The Deshmukh, a hereditary pargana-level official of the Deccan, collected land revenue from the peasants for the state treasury. Chauth was a Maratha levy, not his duty.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.16 (watandar: Desais and Deshmukhs); old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 6

x: Sahyadri geography (security), the Bhakti saints (religious consciousness) and the Marathas' service in the Deccan sultanates (political awakening) all helped their rise, so all of the above is correct.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 0

x: Shivaji was born in 1630 at the hill fort of Shivneri near Pune. Raigad was his capital and coronation fort, and Sinhagad (Kondana) was a later conquest.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127 (born at the hill fort of Shivneri)

x: Maharashtra renamed Aurangabad after Sambhaji, Shivaji's son. The state decided this in 2022 and the name was notified in 2023 as Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, which is the 'Sambhaji Nagar' option.
source: Maharashtra Government gazette (2023) / PIB-reported renaming of Aurangabad as Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar
evidence: Maharashtra cabinet decision June 2022; Union approval Feb 2023 (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar)

x: The key is 1627, 1674: Jadunath Sarkar's birth year, 1627, and the coronation as Chhatrapati at Raigad, 1674. 1661 and 1671 are not his title year.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127, p.129; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 1
dispute: Most books and keys: born 1627 (Jadunath Sarkar). Strictly, the date now accepted (Maharashtra government; PMF) is 19 February 1630.

x: Samarth Ramdas is traditionally Shivaji's guru; he wrote the Dasbodh. Tukaram was a contemporary saint, and Gaga Bhatt was the coronation priest.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 1

x: Shahaji held the Pune jagir as a mansabdar of the Adil Shahi (Bijapur) sultanate after Ahmadnagar fell in 1636. That is the standard key.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127 (Shahaji accepted Adilshahi mansab; his Pune jagir); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shahaji
evidence: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shahaji (Jagirdar of Pune in Bijapur Sultanate)
dispute: Most keys: Adil Shahi (Bijapur). Strictly, the Pune jagir was first granted to Shahaji's father Maloji by the Nizam Shahis (1595), and Shahaji kept it under Bijapur.

x: Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort (1630). Purandar was the treaty fort, Raigad the coronation fort, and Poona his father's jagir.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127

x: Raigad (Raigarh), taken from the Mores of Javli in 1656, was Shivaji's capital and his coronation site (1674).
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.129; old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 1

x: Samarth Ramdas, author of the Dasbodh, is regarded as Shivaji's spiritual guru. Eknath died in 1599, before Shivaji was born, and Namdev was a 14th-century saint (official key printed: Eknath).
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 1

x: Sawai Raja Jai Singh of Amber drew up the Zij Muhammad Shahi, a set of tables for astronomical observation.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.37

x: Torna (1646), taken from Bijapur when Shivaji was 16, was the first fort he captured (the stem's 'port' means fort). Purandar, Kondana and Raigad came later.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 1; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.127

x: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed with the Mughal general Raja Jai Singh of Amber. Shivaji killed Afzal Khan in 1659 and raided Shaista Khan in 1663.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.129; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.13

x: In 1666 Aurangzeb placed Shivaji under house arrest at Agra, from where he escaped with Sambhaji hidden in baskets of fruit and sweets.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.129

x: At Salher (1672) the Marathas defeated the Mughals in open battle. Purandar was a treaty, and Raigarh and Shivneri were forts.
source: old app notes 1:139-141 (old-notes.txt) 140 sub 2

x: Raja Jai Singh of Amber, sent with Diler Khan, besieged Purandar and signed the treaty with Shivaji in 1665. Shaista Khan was the noble raided in 1663.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.129; NextGen Indian History APPSC 05 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-05.txt) p.13

x: Afzal Khan was the general of the Adil Shahi sultan of Bijapur, sent in 1659. Shivaji killed him at the foot of Pratapgad.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-04.txt) p.128

x: Aurangzeb sent his maternal uncle Shaista Khan against Shivaji (1660). Shivaji's night raid on him at Pune in 1663 ended the campaign. Diler Khan came later, with Jai Singh (1665).
